title: Chronic Kidney Disease: Confirm Chronicity, Stage Risk, Slow Progression
bottomLine: CKD requires persistent kidney damage and/or reduced filtration over time, not one abnormal creatinine. Stage using eGFR plus albuminuria, identify reversible/secondary causes and manage blood pressure, diabetes, cardiovascular risk, nephrotoxin exposure and referral risk together.
recognize: CKD may be asymptomatic until advanced; albuminuria can signal important disease even when eGFR is preserved.
Rapid eGFR decline, heavy proteinuria, resistant hypertension or systemic features suggest higher-risk disease.
differentiate: AKI or transient dehydration cannot be labelled CKD from one low eGFR.
Creatinine/eGFR interpretation is affected by muscle mass and non-steady-state physiology.
assessment: Review BP, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, NSAIDs/contrast/nephrotoxins, urinary symptoms, family/systemic disease and volume status.
workup: Confirm chronicity with prior/repeat kidney measures, quantify urine albumin/protein and use urinalysis/imaging/cause-directed serology when indicated.
Use eGFR/albuminuria risk together to guide monitoring and referral.
management: Control BP and diabetes using kidney-protective therapy when indicated, address smoking/lipids and avoid nephrotoxins.
Refer high-risk/progressive or diagnostically uncertain disease to nephrology.
medicationSafety: Dose renally cleared drugs using current kidney function and the drug-specific recommendation.
RAAS blockade/SGLT2 therapy requires expected renal/electrolyte monitoring and should not be stopped reflexively for every small creatinine change.
counselling: Teach sick-day/nephrotoxin precautions where applicable and explain why urine albumin matters even when creatinine looks acceptable.
followUp: Trend eGFR, albuminuria, BP, potassium and complications at a risk-appropriate interval.
examTrap: Diagnosing CKD from one creatinine during dehydration without establishing chronicity.
oneLinePearl: CKD risk lives in both filtration and albuminuria—and it must be chronic.

title: Acute Kidney Injury: Follow the Trend, Urine, and Cause
bottomLine: AKI is a dynamic change in kidney function and/or urine output. Identify prerenal, intrinsic and obstructive causes, stop avoidable nephrotoxins, correct perfusion or obstruction and monitor potassium, acid-base status, volume and symptoms; eGFR equations are unreliable during rapidly changing creatinine.
recognize: Rising creatinine, oliguria, hyperkalemia, acidosis and fluid overload can accompany AKI.
Older/frail patients may have major functional decline with modest absolute creatinine change because baseline muscle mass is low.
differentiate: Prerenal hypoperfusion, intrinsic renal injury and postrenal obstruction can coexist.
CKD with stable abnormal creatinine differs from a new trajectory.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, volume status, urine output, sepsis/bleeding, medications/NSAIDs/RAAS blockers/diuretics, contrast, urinary obstruction and systemic disease.
workup: Trend creatinine/electrolytes/urinalysis and use bladder scan/renal imaging when obstruction is plausible.
Use urine sediment and cause-directed serology when intrinsic renal disease is suspected; avoid relying on calculated eGFR as steady-state truth during active AKI.
management: Restore perfusion without fluid overload, treat sepsis/obstruction, stop or adjust nephrotoxins and dose medications for current function.
Dialysis decisions are driven by refractory complications and clinical status rather than a creatinine threshold alone.
medicationSafety: Potassium-raising/nephrotoxic drugs may need temporary adjustment according to cause/severity.
Avoid indiscriminate fluid boluses in cardiorenal/volume-overloaded patients.
counselling: After recovery, explain medication restart/recheck plans and avoidance of unnecessary nephrotoxins.
followUp: Document post-AKI renal recovery and reassess for CKD when kidney function does not return to baseline.
examTrap: Using a calculated eGFR as if it were reliable while creatinine is changing rapidly.
oneLinePearl: AKI is a trajectory; treat the cause and the complications, not the creatinine number.
sourceBasis: Canadian nephrology acute kidney injury practice

title: Proteinuria: Quantify It, Confirm It, Find the Kidney Risk
bottomLine: Proteinuria is a marker, not a diagnosis. Confirm persistence, quantify albumin/protein accurately and interpret it with eGFR, blood pressure, diabetes, urine sediment and systemic features; heavy or nephritic proteinuria changes referral urgency.
recognize: Albuminuria can precede eGFR decline in diabetes and glomerular disease.
Transient proteinuria can occur with fever, exercise or acute illness.
differentiate: Dipstick protein is semiquantitative and may miss or overstate disease depending on urine concentration and protein type.
Albumin-predominant glomerular disease differs from overflow/nonalbumin proteinuria.
assessment: Assess diabetes/BP, edema, hematuria, systemic autoimmune/infectious symptoms, pregnancy, medications and family history.
workup: Use urine albumin-to-creatinine or protein-to-creatinine ratio as appropriate and repeat to confirm persistent disease outside transient illness.
Use urine microscopy, renal function and cause-directed serology/imaging when the pattern warrants it.
management: Treat the underlying disease and use kidney-protective BP/RAAS/SGLT2 strategies when indicated.
Refer heavy/progressive proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, active sediment or unexplained disease to nephrology.
medicationSafety: RAAS blockade requires potassium/creatinine monitoring and pregnancy avoidance.
NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion and edema.
counselling: Explain that urine protein is an important cardiovascular/kidney risk marker even before symptoms appear.
followUp: Trend quantified albumin/protein and kidney function after treatment rather than repeated dipsticks alone.
examTrap: Calling one positive dipstick chronic kidney disease without confirming or quantifying proteinuria.
oneLinePearl: Proteinuria should be quantified and interpreted with the whole kidney picture.

title: Hematuria: Glomerular, Urologic, or Transient?
bottomLine: Hematuria requires confirmation and localization. Proteinuria, dysmorphic cells/casts and renal dysfunction suggest glomerular disease; painless gross hematuria or cancer-risk features require urologic evaluation; anticoagulation does not eliminate the need to find the source.
recognize: Visible hematuria, persistent microscopic hematuria or hematuria with protein/renal decline deserve different levels of evaluation.
Exercise, menstruation, infection and stones can cause transient blood.
differentiate: Glomerular hematuria often accompanies proteinuria/active sediment; urologic bleeding may be gross/clotted and lacks glomerular features.
Positive dipstick heme can reflect hemoglobin/myoglobin and should be confirmed with microscopy when needed.
assessment: Assess pain, clots, dysuria, stones, smoking/occupational cancer risk, menstruation, anticoagulants, infection/systemic symptoms and renal disease.
workup: Confirm urine microscopy and use culture/protein/renal function plus imaging/cystoscopy or nephrology tests according to the risk/localization.
Repeat a clearly transient low-risk finding only when the clinical pathway supports it rather than indefinitely deferring evaluation.
management: Treat infection/stones when confirmed and refer persistent high-risk urologic or glomerular patterns to the appropriate specialty.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants can magnify bleeding but do not by themselves explain persistent hematuria.
Avoid unnecessary antibiotics for sterile hematuria.
redFlags: Painless gross hematuria in cancer-risk patient
counselling: Explain why even painless blood may require evaluation and why anticoagulation does not make the finding 'normal'.
followUp: Close the loop on cystoscopy/imaging/nephrology testing and document resolution when a transient cause is treated.
examTrap: Blaming persistent hematuria on anticoagulation without investigating the urinary tract or glomerular disease.
oneLinePearl: Hematuria is a source-localization problem before it is a treatment problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association hematuria practice resources

title: Urinary Tract Infection: Treat Symptoms and Host Risk, Not a Culture Alone
bottomLine: UTI is a clinical syndrome supported by urine testing when indicated. Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria except in defined populations, and distinguish uncomplicated cystitis from pyelonephritis, pregnancy, obstruction, catheter/device disease or immunocompromise because host/context changes testing and therapy.
recognize: Dysuria, frequency and urgency without vaginal symptoms can support cystitis.
Older adults should not receive antibiotics for a positive culture plus nonspecific confusion alone without a compatible urinary/systemic infection syndrome.
differentiate: Pyelonephritis adds fever/flank pain/systemic illness and may require culture/stronger disposition assessment.
assessment: Assess fever/flank pain, pregnancy, urinary obstruction/stones, male anatomy, catheter, recurrent infection, renal function and STI/vaginal symptoms.
workup: Use urinalysis/culture according to syndrome and risk; culture pyelonephritis/complicated/recurrent or treatment-failure disease when results can guide therapy.
Avoid screening urine cultures in asymptomatic nonpregnant patients without a specific indication.
management: Use the narrowest effective antibiotic/regimen consistent with current local/Canadian guidance and host factors.
Address obstruction/device/source-control issues rather than relying on antibiotics alone.
medicationSafety: Choose antibiotics with renal, pregnancy, allergy and interaction context.
Avoid fluoroquinolone/broad-spectrum exposure when a safer narrow option is appropriate.
counselling: Explain asymptomatic bacteriuria vs infection and give return precautions for fever/flank pain/vomiting.
followUp: Review cultures when obtained and investigate recurrent patterns when risk/complication warrants it.
examTrap: Treating a positive urine culture in an asymptomatic older adult solely because delirium is present.
oneLinePearl: Treat the urinary syndrome, not the culture result.

title: Pyelonephritis: Identify the Patient Who Needs Imaging, IV Therapy, or Source Control
bottomLine: Pyelonephritis is upper urinary infection with systemic illness. Culture before therapy when feasible, assess sepsis/pregnancy/renal function and obstruction risk, and image/escalate patients with severe illness, stones/obstruction, atypical course or failure rather than ordering CT routinely for every uncomplicated case.
recognize: Fever, flank pain/CVA tenderness, nausea/vomiting and urinary symptoms support the syndrome.
Older/immunocompromised patients may have atypical presentations.
differentiate: Renal colic, appendicitis, PID and lower UTI can overlap.
Obstructive pyelonephritis is a urologic emergency because antibiotics alone cannot drain the infected system.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, hydration, pregnancy, stone/obstruction history, renal function, immunocompromise, prior resistant organisms and ability to tolerate oral therapy.
workup: Obtain urine culture and relevant blood/renal tests; reserve imaging for obstruction/stone concern, severe illness, atypical host or failure to improve.
management: Use empiric antibiotic therapy matched to severity/local susceptibility, then narrow to culture.
Hospitalize/IV treat unstable, pregnant high-risk or unable-to-tolerate patients and urgently decompress obstructed infection.
medicationSafety: Avoid delaying source control by repeatedly broadening antibiotics in obstruction.
counselling: Teach hydration as appropriate, completion of therapy and urgent return for worsening systemic symptoms.
followUp: Review culture/clinical response and evaluate recurrent infections or stone/structural risk as indicated.
examTrap: Ordering CT for every straightforward pyelonephritis—or treating an obstructed infected kidney with antibiotics alone.
oneLinePearl: Pyelonephritis becomes a source-control emergency when infected urine cannot drain.

title: Kidney Stones: Control Pain, Exclude Infection/Obstruction, Prevent the Next One
bottomLine: Renal colic is managed by analgesia and confirmation of stone/obstruction when needed, but fever/sepsis, solitary kidney, AKI, pregnancy or uncontrolled symptoms changes disposition. Recurrent/high-risk stones deserve metabolic prevention rather than repeated emergency-only care.
recognize: Sudden colicky flank pain radiating to groin with hematuria/nausea is typical but not diagnostic.
Stone size/location and patient factors influence passage likelihood and intervention.
differentiate: AAA, ectopic pregnancy, pyelonephritis, ovarian/testicular disease and other abdominal emergencies can mimic colic.
Infected obstruction differs fundamentally from uncomplicated stone passage.
assessment: Assess fever, hemodynamics, urine output, pregnancy, solitary kidney, renal function, prior stones, pain/vomiting and infection risk.
workup: Use urinalysis/renal function and appropriate imaging; ultrasound is preferred in pregnancy and can help reduce radiation in selected patients.
For recurrent/high-risk stones, use stone analysis and metabolic urine/blood evaluation.
management: Provide NSAID/other analgesia when safe, hydration to normal needs and selected medical expulsive therapy according to current urology guidance.
Urgently decompress infected obstruction and refer large/nonpassing/complicated stones.
medicationSafety: Do not force excessive fluids during acute obstruction; it does not guarantee passage and can worsen pain.
counselling: Use stone-specific prevention: adequate fluid, sodium moderation and targeted diet/medication based on stone/metabolic findings.
followUp: Confirm passage/resolution when needed and arrange metabolic prevention for recurrent/high-risk disease.
examTrap: Sending home a febrile patient with an obstructing stone on oral antibiotics without urgent decompression evaluation.
oneLinePearl: A stone plus infection is a drainage emergency; recurrent stones need prevention science.

title: Glomerulonephritis: Recognize the Nephritic Pattern and Refer Before Rapid Loss
bottomLine: Hematuria with proteinuria, active urine sediment, hypertension/edema and declining kidney function should raise glomerulonephritis concern. Confirm the nephritic pattern, identify systemic/infectious clues and involve nephrology urgently when kidney function is deteriorating rather than treating the hematuria as a routine UTI.
recognize: RBC casts/dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria and renal decline suggest glomerular bleeding.
Rash, arthritis, pulmonary symptoms, infection history or systemic autoimmune disease can identify the cause.
differentiate: Lower urinary bleeding lacks glomerular sediment/protein pattern.
Postinfectious, IgA, vasculitic, lupus and anti-GBM disease have different urgency/treatment.
assessment: Assess BP, edema, urine output, respiratory symptoms/hemoptysis, rash/joints, infection history, medications and systemic disease.
workup: Use renal function/electrolytes, quantified protein, urine microscopy and cause-directed complement/autoimmune/infectious testing with nephrology input.
Renal biopsy is specialist-directed when it will define diagnosis/treatment.
management: Control volume/BP and avoid nephrotoxins while arranging urgent nephrology for progressive disease.
Pulmonary-renal syndrome or rapidly progressive GN requires emergency specialty management.
medicationSafety: Do not start empiric immunosuppression without appropriate infection/diagnostic consideration except in specialist-directed emergencies.
RAAS blockade may be useful for proteinuria but requires kidney/potassium context.
counselling: Explain why urine blood plus protein/renal change points to kidney inflammation rather than bladder infection.
followUp: Ensure urgent nephrology testing/biopsy/treatment plans are completed and monitor renal recovery/chronic disease.
examTrap: Treating hematuria/proteinuria/renal decline as recurrent UTI because leukocytes are also present.
oneLinePearl: Blood plus protein plus active sediment points upstream—to the glomerulus.
